header.name: State and Subject: Advanced topics in political anthropology
header.description: This is an advanced class suitable for grad students in the SSH department interested in 'politics'. If you are an undergraduate student, consider taking SOC216 instead.(Also, SOC216 is an anti-requisite for this class) This course is an examination of the relationship between 'state' and 'subject', key categories of 'politics'. We begin from 'outside' the state: a 'head' less, or stateless society, and a 'society against state'. We then study pre-modern 'kingship' traversing 3 cases - 1)the Balinese 'Negara' from pre-colonial times (Geertz), 2)the political theology of the English King's 'two bodies' - a natural body that is born, grows old and dies, and an eternal 'body politic' (Kantorowicz), and 3) the composition of sovereignty in a South Indian 'Little Kingdom' before and during English colonisation (Dirks). This draws the 'pre-modern' section to a close. We enter the modern, with the problem of 'governing' the population. We study different practices of the modern project of administrative order, including bureaucratic record keeping, the ordering of social space which in turn requires techniques of 'representing' society. We then examine the category that lies at the heart of the modern political state - the 'citizen' who, as a member of the community of citizens is declared to be an 'egalitarian sovereign' - a contradiction in terms. We study this contradiction through an important debate in political philosophy - a critique of the political relationship between 'religion' and 'state' (Marx's Jewish Question). We proceed further into the contradiction, through an examination of 'equality' and 'liberty' - the key 'rights' that are constitutive of the citizen, but rights that no institution can guarantee in a stable way. We see how this instability at the heart of constitutive politics is productive of an excess that necessitates the other central modern political form of oppositional or insurrectionary politics. We look at a case study of the insurrectionary (revolutionary) political form and the relationship between 'the military' and 'the political' (Regis Debray on Che and Castro). Next we examine problems of subjection at the 'margins' of the state, where the sovereignty of the 'modern' state is produced in 'magical' ways, taking us back to the contradictions at the heart of the category of 'citizen'. Finally, we close with a critique of the liberal democratic model of politics, through the concept of 'the political' - of politics as the distinction between 'friend' and 'enemy', an 'us' and a 'them'. By the end of the class, students will develop dexterity over a set of concepts, to model questions of politics they encounter in their research.

outcomes.label: CO2

lecture_topics: Asiatic Kingship - pomp and power (Geertz - Negara)
European Kingship - the king's two bodies (Kantorowicz)
The people' - Roussaeu and enlightenment politics
Contradictions of citizenship - The Jewish question (Marx)
Contradictions of the contract - Equaliberty and the Citizen Subject (Balibar)
Revolution in the Revolution - Regis debray on insurrection (Guerilla war and politics)
Law, legitimacy and sovereignty - margins of the state (Das, Jeganathan)
Critique of the liberal position - 'The Political' (Schmitt and Mouffe)
